sections.h2: Choosing how to sell in Tamarac
sections.html:
Match the route to your deadline: a listing for the widest market, an as-is investor sale for speed, or a cash offer when you want the fewest steps. Tamarac is a compact Broward County city of about 74,134 people, with 76.2% of homes owner-occupied and a typical owned-home value of $288,600. Most sales are condos, villas and single-family houses on small lots, and buyers compare them closely.

A tidy plan for paperwork matters as much as the buyer you choose. Many long-time owners sell for health, family or estate reasons, so the first steps are often the same: payoff figure, association papers, title check.

sections.h2: Seasonal owners selling from a distance
sections.html: Tamarac has long drawn snowbirds as well as year-round residents. Owners who go north for the summer often sell from afar. If that is you, line up a local contact who can meet the buyer, a signing method that works remotely, and a plan for the utilities until closing.

Houses and villas from the early decades often have small floor plans, shared walls or community amenities, and sometimes an association that still handles exterior work. Buyers will ask what the association covers and what it charges.

  • Collect the association's rules, budget and any pending special assessment.
  • Ask the association how long its approval or estoppel letter takes.
  • Gather records for the roof, windows and air conditioning, since buyers price those first.

A seller with these ready can answer a cash buyer within a day instead of a week. Without them, an offer can sit for weeks waiting on the association.

sections.h2: What a Tamarac seller pays at closing
sections.html:
Broward uses the standard deed rate of $0.70 per $100, since only Miami-Dade differs (Department of Revenue).

  • Deed tax, collected by the clerk when recording.
  • Recording fees under s. 28.24.
  • The seller's share of the year's property tax.
  • Payoff of any loan or lien.

Add association charges and an estoppel letter fee if your community requires them. The contract decides who pays deed tax, but every party stays liable.

The Broward County Property Appraiser sets values and exemptions, and the office answers at 954-357-6830 on weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm. A buyer does not inherit your capped assessment, since a change of ownership resets it the next January 1.

A homestead cap holds yearly growth to the lower of 3 percent or CPI (Department of Revenue), which is why a long-held Tamarac house can carry a bill far under a new owner's. The calendar is on the state tax page.

Deferred tax is repaid at sale, so request a payoff figure early.

sections.h2: Keeping your Save Our Homes benefit
sections.html: Part of it can move with you through portability. Set up the next homestead within three years of January 1 of the year you left this one, and file Form DR-501T with the DR-501 by March 1 (guide). The clock starts from the January 1 date, not the closing.

sections.h2: Owner has died or the house is inherited
sections.html: A personal representative must be named before a sale, unless the estate fits summary administration (s. 735.201). Lady bird deeds are a different tool, and the Department of Revenue has advised that one such deed carried no stamp tax on its facts. Have a Florida attorney read your deed.

sections.h2: Owing more than the house is worth
sections.html: Speak to the lender early. Selling before a court sale lets you choose the buyer and the date. Foreclosure sales follow judgment within 20 to 35 days unless extended (s. 45.031).

Compare net proceeds, timeline and risk, and ask every buyer the same questions.

  • How many days from signed contract to closing?
  • Does the offer depend on financing or inspection?
  • Who pays title insurance and deed tax?
  • Does the written offer match the verbal one?

Steady demand on a small, fixed amount of land means competition for homes, and a seller can use it. Still, an offer is only worth what reaches you at the table.

A cash buyer has no loan to be approved, so the lender's appraisal and underwriting steps drop out and a sale cannot collapse because financing fell through. The rest of the process stays: title search, payoff of liens and mortgages, a signed deed, and recording with the Broward County clerk.

Cash buyers also tend to take a house as it is. Skipping repairs, staging and showings is the real saving of time, and the offer reflects it. If your community has an association, remember that the buyer's closing still waits on the association's paperwork, so order it the day you accept an offer.

1. Accept an offer and sign the contract, naming who pays title insurance and deed tax.
  2. Request the association's estoppel letter and sale documents.
  3. The title company searches the records for liens, mortgages and ownership problems.
  4. Collect payoff figures from the servicer and, if you deferred taxes, from the tax collector.
  5. Sign the deed with two witnesses, and the clerk records it.

Most delays come from one of three things: a slow association, a missing owner signature, or a lien nobody knew about. A title search early in the week takes care of the third, and a quick call to every owner on the deed takes care of the second.

A buyer will want to see what you have, and a seller who answers fast usually gets a better offer. Pull together the recorded deed, your latest Broward County tax bill, proof of any exemption, the association's rules and budget, and invoices for the roof, windows and air conditioning.

If you hold a homestead exemption, say so, and remind the buyer that the exemption does not transfer. They file their own application by March 1, and the assessment resets after the sale. Telling them early avoids a surprise when their first bill arrives and looks higher than yours.
Land deeds need two witnesses, and every owner must sign. Settle any missing signature before the closing date.

sections.h2: Four calls to make this week
sections.html:
Start with four calls, in this order.

  1. Your mortgage servicer, for a payoff figure.
  2. Your association, for its sale requirements and fees.
  3. A title company, for a preliminary look at liens and ownership.
  4. Two or three buyers, for written offers you can compare.

Doing these in one week gives you a full picture of the net you can expect, and it keeps any deadline from sneaking up on you.

faqs.q: Can I sell for cash in Tamarac if the house is in a homeowners association?
faqs.a: Yes, but the association may require an application or estoppel letter. Request the documents early because the buyer cannot close without them.

faqs.q: Will Broward County tax bills change after I sell?
faqs.a: Yes, for the buyer. The assessment resets after a change of ownership.

faqs.q: What deed tax rate applies in Tamarac?
faqs.a: It is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, the standard rate outside Miami-Dade. The contract decides who pays, but all parties remain liable.

faqs.q: Can I sell while behind on the mortgage?
faqs.a: Yes. Until a court sale is confirmed you can sell and pay the lender at closing.

faqs.q: Does selling end my homestead exemption?
faqs.a: The exemption ends for that property. You can reapply on a new Florida home by March 1, and you may be able to carry over part of your capped value through portability.
